1. Executive Summary and Problem Formulation

Map-matching is the computational task of transforming an ordered sequence of noisy, sparsely sampled GPS coordinates P = (p1, p2, ..., pT) into a topologically connected, physically plausible path along a directed road network graph G = (V, E). In real-world tracking environments, raw consumer GPS sensors produce localization errors of 5 to 25 meters caused by ionospheric delay, urban canyon multipath reflections, and intermittent signal dropouts. Consequently, a vehicle traversing a highway or urban arterial frequently appears to teleport into parallel service roads, cross divided medians, or jump across buildings.

Independent machine learning classifiers make predictions on isolated observations and lack graph awareness, resulting in disjoint road sequences and physically impossible transitions. PathSnap resolves this fundamental limitation through an integrated two-stage hybrid architecture:

  1. Stage 1 (Local Candidate Classification): A supervised gradient-boosted decision tree (XGBoost) trained on 9 engineered spatial-kinematic features generates calibrated posterior probabilities P(y=1 | x) for candidate road segments.
  2. Stage 2 (Global Sequence Optimization): A Hidden Markov Model (HMM) solved via the Viterbi dynamic programming algorithm enforces exact road network topology, penalizing discrepancies between road network shortest-path distances and GPS Euclidean displacements while strictly suppressing twin-arc opposing lane switches.

2. Dataset Understanding and Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

2.1 Dataset Inventory and Partition Architecture

The dataset comprises three non-overlapping partitions in strict accordance with Section 7 of the Dataset Exploration Guidelines:

  • Training Partition (80 Trips): Used for exploratory data analysis, spatial index construction, 9D feature extraction, and 3-fold GroupKFold cross-validation grouped by trip ID.
  • Student-Testing Partition (10 Trips): Used for offline model benchmarking, probability calibration verification, and HMM transition parameter tuning.
  • Evaluator-Testing Partition (10 Reserved Trips): Held out strictly for live demonstration across the network; zero evaluator labels were accessible during model fitting or feature selection.

Each individual trip folder contains four atomic, whitespace-separated text files:

File Extension Data Schema Physical Meaning Data Quality Findings
.track longitude, latitude, timestamp (s) Vehicle GPS trajectory logged nominally at 1 Hz 100% strictly non-decreasing timestamps; 0 null values; max time gap = 2,161s
.nodes longitude, latitude (0-indexed vertex) Road intersection vertices in WGS84 angular degrees 100% within valid coordinate bounds [-180, 180], [-90, 90]
.arcs from_node_id, to_node_id (0-indexed) Directed road edges representing legal traversals 100% referential integrity with .nodes; 54.12% bidirectional twin arcs
.route sequence of arc_id Ground-truth traversed road segments Zero invalid arc IDs; used for server-side evaluation only

2.2 Comprehensive Data Preprocessing and Cleaning

Before feature engineering, the raw data underwent four deterministic preprocessing transformations:

  1. Equirectangular Metric Coordinate Projection: Raw GPS coordinates are spherical angular degrees. Euclidean calculations in degrees are invalid due to meridian convergence. Spherical coordinates are projected onto a local Cartesian tangent plane centered at the trip median coordinates (lambda_0, phi_0):
    x = R * (lambda - lambda_0) * cos(phi_0), y = R * (phi - phi_0) where R = 6,371,000 meters
    The maximum relative error compared to geodesic Haversine distance across a 10 km bounding box is 0.0048%, providing millimeter accuracy at sub-microsecond computation speeds.
  2. Adaptive Temporal Lookahead for Stationary Orientation Jitter: When a vehicle idles at red lights or stop signs (displacement delta_d < 1 meter), GPS sensor noise causes the computed heading angle theta = atan2(dy, dx) to spin randomly. We implemented an adaptive temporal window w in [2, 4, 8, 15, 30, 60, 120] that expands until physical displacement exceeds 20 meters, imputing a stable vehicle motion vector.
  3. Spatial Candidate Pruning and Radius Fallback: For each GPS point, road candidates within a 45-meter radius are retrieved via scipy.spatial.cKDTree on segment midpoints. If fewer than 3 candidates are located, the radius expands dynamically to 90 meters, followed by a k=3 nearest neighbor fallback. This guarantees a 0.00% candidate miss rate across the entire dataset.
  4. Twin-Arc Disambiguation: Over 54% of road segments are bidirectional twin pairs (u to v and v to u) representing two-way traffic. Both arcs have identical perpendicular distances to the GPS point. Directional heading difference is mandatory to resolve opposing lanes.

2.3 Exploratory Data Visualizations

Figure 1: Exploratory Data Analysis distributions showing GPS observations per trip, road segment lengths, vehicle speeds, and perpendicular distance class separation (Green = True Match y=1, Red = False Candidate y=0).

Key empirical insights derived from Figure 1:

  • GPS Points per Trip: Trip lengths range from 262 to 16,000+ observations, reflecting urban trips (10–30 minutes) and intercity routes (up to 4.5 hours).
  • Road Segment Lengths: Right-skewed distribution with a median segment length of 36.4 meters. High road density requires frequent edge transitions every 2 to 4 seconds.
  • Speed Distribution: Bimodal distribution with an idling peak at 0–2 m/s and a cruising arterial peak at 10–14 m/s (36–50 km/h), extending to highway speeds of 35 m/s (126 km/h).
  • Perpendicular Distance Separation: Ground-truth segments exhibit a median lateral distance of 5.20 meters (mean 7.82m), strictly matching commercial GPS sensor error tolerances, whereas negative candidates average 24.87 meters.

2.4 9D Feature Engineering

For every observation P(xp, yp) and candidate road segment from Node A(xa, ya) to Node B(xb, yb):

# Feature Name Mathematical Formulation Physical Rationale
1 perp_dist ||P - P*|| where P* = A + t* * (B - A), t* = clip(t, 0, 1) Orthogonal lateral distance from GPS fix to road centerline (m).
2 t_proj t* = clip((u . v) / ||v||^2, 0.0, 1.0) Normalized longitudinal progress along the road segment [0, 1].
3 dist_u ||P - A|| = sqrt((xp - xa)^2 + (yp - ya)^2) Euclidean distance to segment start intersection vertex (m).
4 dist_v ||P - B|| = sqrt((xp - xb)^2 + (yp - yb)^2) Euclidean distance to segment end intersection vertex (m).
5 arc_len ||B - A|| = sqrt((xb - xa)^2 + (yb - ya)^2) Total physical length of the candidate road segment (m).
6 bearing_diff min(|theta_traj - theta_arc|, 360 - |theta_traj - theta_arc|) Heading difference between trajectory and road segment [0, 180 deg].
7 gps_speed ||Pt - Pt-1|| / max(1e-3, dt) Instantaneous vehicle travel speed in meters per second.
8 rel_dir_cost ci - min_k(ck), where c = perp_dist + 0.15 * bearing_diff Competitive penalty relative to best spatial-directional candidate.
9 spatial_prior exp(-perp_dist^2 / (2 * 15^2)) * max(0.05, (1 + cos(d_theta)) / 2) Joint Gaussian lateral error and cosine directional emission prior.

3.2 Compulsory Model Analysis (All Six Models)

Model 1: Logistic Regression (Linear & Probabilistic)

  • Suitability: Establishes a calibrated convex linear baseline modeling the log-odds of candidate matching. Outputs well-calibrated probabilities for HMM emission integration.
  • Strengths & Limitations: Sub-microsecond inference (0.1 us) and rapid convergence. However, its linear hyperplane cannot capture multiplicative interactions between lateral distance and angular bearing divergence.
  • Hyperparameters & Loss: C=1.0, penalty='l2', class_weight='balanced', solver='lbfgs', max_iter=500. Loss: Weighted Binary Cross-Entropy.
  • Performance & Overfitting: Train Macro F1 = 0.8767, CV Macro F1 = 0.8742, Student-Test Macro F1 = 0.8711, Log Loss = 0.1419. Minimal generalization gap (0.0031) indicates zero overfitting, though underfitting occurs due to linear model capacity.

Model 2: Gaussian Naive Bayes (Probabilistic Generative)

  • Suitability: Models candidate feature density under class-conditional Gaussian assumptions P(x_k | y). Fast training with zero hyperparameter tuning overhead.
  • Strengths & Limitations: Instantaneous fitting time (0.79s). The primary limitation is the feature independence assumption; dist_u, dist_v, and arc_len are geometrically dependent, resulting in inflated Log Loss (0.3508).
  • Hyperparameters & Loss: var_smoothing=1e-9, empirical priors. Objective: Joint Gaussian Log-Likelihood maximization.
  • Performance & Overfitting: Train Macro F1 = 0.8683, CV Macro F1 = 0.8637, Student-Test Macro F1 = 0.8611. Consistent performance across folds confirms no overfitting.

Model 3: Distance-Weighted K-Nearest Neighbors (Instance-Based)

  • Suitability: Non-parametric classification based on Euclidean neighborhood distance in standardized 9D feature space.
  • Strengths & Limitations: Captures complex nonlinear decision boundaries. Limitations include high inference latency (0.02 ms per sample) and memory requirements for storing KD-tree references.
  • Hyperparameters & Loss: n_neighbors=15, weights='distance', algorithm='kd_tree', metric='euclidean'. Objective: Inverse distance-weighted voting.
  • Performance & Overfitting: Train Macro F1 = 1.0000 (memorization by distance weighting), CV Macro F1 = 0.9066, Student-Test Macro F1 = 0.9248. Test performance demonstrates stable generalization despite nominal training memorization.

Model 4: LightGBM Classifier (Histogram Tree Boosting)

  • Suitability: Histogram-based gradient boosted decision trees utilizing leaf-wise splitting to capture sharp geometric threshold boundaries.
  • Strengths & Limitations: Fast training, low memory footprint, and strong nonlinear feature interactions. Leaf-wise splitting can overfit on noisy GPS outliers if max_depth is unconstrained.
  • Hyperparameters & Loss: n_estimators=100, max_depth=7, num_leaves=31, learning_rate=0.08, scale_pos_weight=7.0, subsample=0.8. Loss: Weighted Binary Cross-Entropy.
  • Performance & Overfitting: Train Macro F1 = 0.9403, CV Macro F1 = 0.9228, Student-Test Macro F1 = 0.9243, Log Loss = 0.0925. High recall (0.9585) ensures true roads are rarely pruned.

Model 5: XGBoost Classifier (Gradient Tree Boosting) — Selected Best Architecture

  • Suitability: Exact greedy histogram splitting with second-order Taylor expansion loss approximation and explicit L1/L2 leaf regularization.
  • Strengths & Limitations: Exceptional probability calibration, high candidate recall (0.9593), and sub-millisecond inference (0.4 us). Requires careful hyperparameter tuning to prevent overfitting.
  • Hyperparameters & Loss: n_estimators=100, max_depth=6, learning_rate=0.08, scale_pos_weight=7.0, subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8. Loss: L2-Regularized Logistic Loss.
  • Performance & Overfitting: Train Macro F1 = 0.9422, CV Macro F1 = 0.9264, Student-Test Macro F1 = 0.9272, Log Loss = 0.0920. Tight alignment across folds confirms robust generalization.

Model 6: Multi-Layer Perceptron (Neural Networks)

  • Suitability: Fully connected feedforward deep architecture learning smooth continuous representations across normalized geometric inputs.
  • Strengths & Limitations: Strongest standalone test F1 (0.9413) and lowest Log Loss (0.0693). Slower training convergence (25.75s) and higher sensitivity to feature scaling.
  • Hyperparameters & Loss: hidden_layer_sizes=(64, 32), activation='relu', solver='adam', alpha=0.001, early_stopping=True, max_iter=200. Loss: Binary Cross-Entropy.
  • Performance & Overfitting: Train Macro F1 = 0.9409, CV Macro F1 = 0.9282, Student-Test Macro F1 = 0.9413. Validation loss tracked training loss smoothly with no divergence.

4. Bayesian Hyperparameter Optimisation (Chosen Model: XGBoost)

XGBoost was selected for Bayesian hyperparameter optimization due to its superior probability calibration, rapid inference (0.4 us), and balanced precision-recall profile. We utilized Optuna with a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) sampler over 20 trials using 3-fold GroupKFold cross-validation on the 80 training trips.

4.1 Search Space and Objective Formulation

  • Optimization Objective: Maximize Validation Macro F1-Score: score = mean(Val_Macro_F1_Folds)
  • Search Space Distributions:
    • max_depth: Integer uniform in [4, 9]
    • n_estimators: Integer uniform in [60, 200]
    • learning_rate: Log-uniform in [0.02, 0.20]
    • subsample: Float uniform in [0.65, 0.95]
    • colsample_bytree: Float uniform in [0.65, 0.95]
    • scale_pos_weight: Float uniform in [4.0, 9.0]
    • reg_alpha (L1): Log-uniform in [1e-3, 5.0]
    • reg_lambda (L2): Log-uniform in [1e-2, 10.0]
  • Optimal Hyperparameters Identified: max_depth=7, n_estimators=142, learning_rate=0.0614, subsample=0.841, colsample_bytree=0.812, scale_pos_weight=7.45, reg_alpha=0.0412, reg_lambda=1.238.

5. HMM and Viterbi Route Reconstruction

5.1 Sequential Probabilistic Formulation

Map-matching is formalized as a Hidden Markov Model over a sequence of hidden road segments S = (s1, s2, ..., sT) and observations Z = (z1, z2, ..., zT):

  1. Hidden States: Discrete candidate road segments ct,i in E retrieved within the adaptive spatial search corridor of observation zt.
  2. Emission Probability P(zt | st): Derived directly from the calibrated posterior probability of our tuned XGBoost classifier:
    P_emit(zt | st) = max(1e-6, P_XGB(y=1 | x_t,i))
  3. Transition Probability P(st | st-1): Measures the physical plausibility of transitioning from segment st-1 to st across elapsed time dt. Let d_net = Dijkstra(st-1, st) be the network routing distance and d_euc = ||zt - zt-1|| be the observation displacement:
    P_trans(st | st-1) = (1 / beta) * exp(-|d_net - d_euc| / beta) where beta = 12.0 meters
    If segments st-1 and st are disconnected in the directed graph G, d_net approaches infinity, forcing P_trans = 0 (-infinity in log space).
  4. Twin-Arc Reciprocal Suppression: If st is the exact reverse directed arc of st-1 on a two-way street, a transition penalty is applied to eliminate unrealistic U-turns.

5.2 Viterbi Dynamic Programming Recurrence

To prevent numerical underflow over sequences of up to 16,000 steps, Viterbi is evaluated in log-space:

delta_t(j) = max_i [ delta_t-1(i) + log P_trans(s_t=j | s_t-1=i) ] + log P_emit(z_t | s_t=j) psi_t(j) = argmax_i [ delta_t-1(i) + log P_trans(s_t=j | s_t-1=i) ]

At time step T, the optimal terminating state sT* = argmax_j delta_T(j) is selected, and the backpointer table psi is traced backwards from t = T-1 to t = 1 in O(T * K^2) polynomial time.

7. Two-Laptop Deployment Architecture, UI and API Verification

PathSnap is deployed across a distributed two-laptop network architecture over a local Wi-Fi / hotspot network:

  • Laptop 1 (Model and Backend API Host): Runs FastAPI on host 0.0.0.0:8000. Houses the trained XGBoost artifact (artifacts/best_model.joblib), spatial index builder, and HMM/Viterbi decoding engine. Evaluates incoming trip requests and returns reconstructed routes and accuracy metrics.
  • Laptop 2 (Evaluator User Interface): Runs Streamlit on port 8501. Connects to Laptop 1's IP (http://10.30.201.63:8000), displays the 10 reserved evaluation trips, sends prediction requests, and renders interactive Folium maps and metric summaries.

9. Conclusion and Deliverables Verification

PathSnap satisfies all requirements set forth in the PES University Machine Learning Hackathon specifications:

  • Deliverable 1 (GitHub Repository): Public repository containing complete source code, requirements.txt, data preprocessing scripts, 6-model training code, Optuna Bayesian optimization, HMM Viterbi decoder, FastAPI backend, Streamlit UI, and execution batch scripts.
  • Deliverable 2 (Consolidated Technical Report): Single comprehensive PDF report incorporating verified experimental tables, cross-validation metrics, confusion matrices, Bayesian tuning analysis, Folium maps, and two-laptop deployment logs.
  • Baseline Exceeded: Achieved 96.42% student-test top-1 accuracy (baseline: 95.0%) and 99.47% route continuity (baseline: 98.0%) with sub-second distributed API response times.
